extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political communication, journalists, politicians, and scholars of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance on how public opinion and a common will are formed from diverse private impressions, and practical techniques leaders and communicators use to unite heterogeneous audiences. Emphasizes symbols, rhetoric, conditioning, and the limits of deterministic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic determinism is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The socialist practice is based on a belief that if men are economically situated in different ways, they can then be induced to hold certain views... The economic determinist cannot tell. A man's various economic contacts limit or enlarge the range of his opinions. But which of the contacts, in what guise, on what theory, the materialistic conception of politics cannot predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume one-to-one mapping from class or economic position to opinion. Economic position makes some outcomes probable (e.g., owners will resist deprivation of ownership), but it does not predict the specific content, breadth, or time-horizon of opinions. Special inquiry is required to discover which economic relation is operative for a given opinion; crude class-based forecasts (as in Marxist determinism) will frequently be wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class interest is variable and not fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fixed set of opinions on any question that go with being the owner of a factory... That theory assumes the existence of a specific class interest. That assumption is false. A class interest can be conceived largely or narrowly, selfishly or unselfishly, in the light of no facts, some facts, many facts, truth and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or trying to mobilize a 'class', treat the notion of class interest as contestable and multi‑interpretable. Policies that assume communal ownership will remove absolute conflicts but will not eliminate divergent conceptions of interest — expect new or residual conflicts unless a shared interpretation is cultivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instincts and dispositions are malleable by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the equipment at birth, the innate dispositions are from earliest infancy immersed in experience which determines what shall excite them as stimulus... 'They become capable... of being initiated... by ideas of such objects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat instinctive reactions as immutable guides to behavior. Psychological and anthropological evidence indicate that stimuli and gratifications associated with instincts are learned and can be redirected; persuasion and education can alter which objects excite an instinctive response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders exploit 'binders' or stereotypes to transfer prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: The italicized words are binders: Lincoln in such a speech has of course no relation to Abraham Lincoln. It is merely a stereotype by which the piety which surrounds that name can be transferred to the Republican candidate who now stands in his shoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create unity among factions, invoke revered names, historical figures, or stereotypes that carry desirable qualities; these 'binders' transfer the prestige and emotion associated with the name to the present candidate or cause. Use with care: the binder's resonance depends on shared cultural meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select non‑explosive opening subjects to avoid division
rubrics_metrics.description: It was necessary to find an opening subject which would not only ignore 1912 but would avoid also the explosive conflicts of 1916... The speaker skilfully selected the spoils system in diplomatic appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling a coalition, begin with issues that are unlikely to rekindle deep schisms. An opening subject should placate multiple factions and serve as a bridge to broader unity. Tactical choice of safe topics helps reframe the audience before addressing more contentious matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ambiguous, multi‑meaning language to encompass factions
rubrics_metrics.description: By letting the words mean all things to all men... the speech passes for a while to safer ground. The theme 'friendship' is for the non‑interventionists, the theme 'new policy' and 'firmness' is for the interventionists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity and polyvalent phrasing let different audience segments read their own values into the same statement, creating apparent agreement while deferring specific conflict. This is an intentional rhetorical technique to form coalitions from diverse beliefs; however, it risks later divergence when specifics are demanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an issue cannot be compromised, obliterate or sidestep it
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus, what cannot be compromised must be obliterated, when there is a question on which we cannot all hope to get together, let us pretend that it does not exist." (example: the Lusitania)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a factual or moral point is irreconcilable among target groups, leaders may neutralize its divisiveness by omission, redefinition, or by reframing the conversation. This suppresses immediate conflict but may leave latent disagreement that resurfaces later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific factual narrative where detail will not arouse contrary passions
rubrics_metrics.description: On the non‑contentious record, the detail is overwhelming; on the issue everything is cloudy... The candidate tells the story of Tampico, Vera Cruz... No contrary passions could be aroused by such a record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed, factual accounts can placate or distract from contentious interpretive disputes when those facts are unlikely to inflame opposing passions. Use specificity to consolidate agreement on background matters while postponing controversy over interpretation or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions can be conditioned and transferred to symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: By what is known to psychologists as conditioned response, an emotion is not attached merely to one idea... If you can find a stimulus which will arouse the same emotion in many of them, you can substitute it for the original stimuli... Suppose that symbol is Americanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach shared emotions (fear, pride, indignation) to versatile symbols so that different constituencies can interpret the symbol in ways compatible with their prior attachments. Designing symbols that evoke the same emotion across groups is a central technique for coalition‑building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols act as truce/junctions and control public feeling; capture them
rubrics_metrics.description: They do not stand for specific ideas, but for a sort of truce or junction between ideas... He who captures the symbols by which public feeling is for the moment contained, controls by that much the approaches of public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Securing dominant symbols (e.g., 'Lincoln', 'Americanism', 'Justice') gives a leader or group strategic control over the framing of debates. But symbols have limits: excessive abuse or mismatch with reality can 'burst' them (example: Holy Russia bursting under defeat), so manage symbols responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit modern mass communication to synchronize ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourteen Points were an attempt to exploit the modern machinery of communication to start the return to a 'common consciousness' throughout the world... Without cable, radio, telegraph, and daily press, the experiment of the Fourteen Points would have been impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available communication technologies to present the same names and ideas simultaneously to wide audiences, thereby increasing the chance of forming shared impressions or a 'common will'. Coordinated messaging across media accelerates crystallization of public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion often simplifies to the least common denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: For the least common denominator of all the votes was that the Democrats should go and the Republicans come in. That was the only factor remaining after all the contradictions had cancelled each other out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that, from many conflicting motives, public action will often emerge from the simplest, widely shared preference rather than nuanced policy positions. Campaigns can aim to identify and amplify such lowest‑common‑denominator drivers to produce decisive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: People substitute shorthand names and signs; guard against verbalism
rubrics_metrics.description: He employs a shorthand of names and signs and samples... But if he forgets that he has substituted and simplified, he soon lapses into verbalism, and begins to talk about names regardless of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicators should be aware that audiences and leaders use names/symbols as cognitive shortcuts. Avoid confusing the symbol with the underlying reality; critics and policymakers should guard against mistaking verbal consensus for substantive understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment audiences by susceptibility to ideas and tailor stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: People differ widely in their susceptibility to ideas. There are some in whom the idea of a starving child in Russia is practically as vivid as a starving child within sight. There are others who are almost incapable of being excited by a distant idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate messaging according to how various groups respond to distant or abstract stimuli. Some will be moved by symbolic appeals, others require concrete, proximate triggers; effective persuasion adapts the stimulus to the audience's sensitivity.
